Direct vs. indirect rollover: why the 60-day rule and 20% withholding trip people up

A direct rollover moves your retirement money straight from one account to another, so no check is made out to you and nothing is withheld. In an indirect rollover the money is paid to you first, and you have 60 days to deposit it; from an employer plan, 20% is withheld for taxes up front.

By Luay Sadqi, Licensed Agent (NPN 21370662) · November 2026

Most rollover mistakes are not about picking the wrong investment. They happen in the handoff, when the money lands in your hands instead of going straight to the next account. This guide explains the two rollover methods, the deadline, and the withholding surprise. It follows the IRS's published rules on rollovers of retirement plan and IRA distributions. It is general information, not tax advice.

Direct rollover: the money never touches you

In a direct rollover, your old plan or IRA sends the money straight to the new account. Depending on the provider, that might be a wire, an electronic transfer, or a check made payable to the new custodian for your benefit rather than to you. Because the money is never distributed to you, a direct rollover between like accounts is generally not taxable and has no mandatory withholding.

Indirect rollover: where the trouble starts

In an indirect (or 60-day) rollover, the plan pays the money to you. You then have 60 days to deposit it into another eligible retirement account. Two things go wrong most often.

1. The 20% withholding gap

When an eligible rollover distribution is paid to you from an employer plan such as a 401(k), the plan generally must withhold 20% for federal income tax, even if you intend to roll it over. To roll over the full amount, you must make up the withheld portion from other money. Here is a simple illustration, not a forecast: if your account is $10,000, you receive $8,000 in cash. To avoid tax on the rest, you would need to deposit the full $10,000 within 60 days. Anything you do not redeposit is generally treated as a taxable distribution, and if you are under 59½, a 10% additional tax may also apply. You can claim the withheld amount back when you file your tax return, but only after the fact.

2. The 60-day clock

The 60 days generally start the day you receive the money. Miss it and the distribution is generally taxable. The IRS can waive the deadline in limited cases, including a self-certification process for certain reasons beyond your control, but a waiver is not guaranteed and it is not a plan to rely on.

Quick comparison
  • Direct: money goes account to account, no withholding on a like-for-like rollover, no deadline stress.
  • Indirect: money is paid to you, 20% is withheld when it comes from an employer plan, and you have 60 days to redeposit.
  • The IRS limits IRA-to-IRA indirect rollovers to one per 12-month period across all of your IRAs.

The one-per-year limit

For IRA-to-IRA indirect rollovers, the IRS generally allows only one in any 12-month period, and the limit counts all your IRAs together, including SEP and SIMPLE IRAs. Direct transfers between custodians and rollovers from an employer plan to an IRA are generally not counted. Break the rule and the second distribution can become taxable. See the IRS page above for the current list of exceptions.

Why a direct rollover is usually the safer path

  • No mandatory withholding to make up out of pocket.
  • No 60-day deadline to track.
  • Fewer chances for a check to be lost, misdirected or deposited into the wrong kind of account.
  • The one-per-year IRA rule is generally not triggered.

An indirect rollover is sometimes used on purpose, for example as a short-term bridge, but it carries the risks above. Ask your current plan administrator for its exact steps, and keep records of every distribution and deposit.

Roth money and annuity rollovers

Rolling pre-tax money into a Roth account is a taxable conversion, not a plain rollover, so check with a tax professional first. If you are considering moving retirement money into an annuity, the same method question applies. Annuities are not investments in the stock market, may carry surrender charges and fees, and guarantees depend on the issuing company's claims-paying ability. See our guide to 401(k) and IRA rollovers into annuities and what to do with your 401(k) when you leave a job.

Questions to ask before you move money

  • Can this be done as a direct rollover or trustee-to-trustee transfer?
  • If a check is issued, who is the payee, and where is it mailed?
  • Is any tax being withheld, and at what rate?
  • Is any part of my balance a required minimum distribution, which cannot be rolled over?

Common questions

Rollover FAQ

Is a direct rollover taxable?
A direct rollover from a traditional account into another traditional account is generally not taxable by itself, and nothing is withheld. Taxes can apply if you convert pre-tax money to a Roth account. A tax professional can tell you how your situation works.
What happens if I miss the 60-day deadline?
The distribution generally counts as taxable income, and if you are under 59 and a half, an additional 10% tax may apply. The IRS can waive the deadline in limited situations, including through self-certification for certain reasons beyond your control, so check IRS guidance or ask a tax professional right away.
Can I do more than one indirect rollover a year?
For IRA-to-IRA indirect rollovers, the IRS generally allows one per 12-month period across all of your IRAs. Direct transfers between custodians and plan-to-IRA rollovers are not limited by that rule, which is another reason to use a direct rollover.
